courses.title: Haemostasis, Thrombosis and Haematological Malignancies
courses.description: Physiology and laboratory investigation of haemostasis, bleeding and thrombotic disorders, anticoagulant monitoring, and laboratory diagnosis of leukaemias, lymphomas and myeloma.

topics.title: Physiology of Haemostasis
topics.summary: Vascular and platelet phases, the coagulation cascade and cell-based model, natural anticoagulants and fibrinolysis.

material.heading: Primary haemostasis
material.body: Haemostasis stops bleeding while keeping blood fluid. After vessel injury: vasoconstriction; platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen via von Willebrand factor (vWF) binding platelet glycoprotein Ib (GPIb); platelet activation (shape change, release of ADP and thromboxane A2 from granules); and aggregation via fibrinogen bridging activated GPIIb/IIIa receptors, forming the primary platelet plug. Normal platelet count is 150–400 × 10⁹/L; lifespan about 7–10 days. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclo-oxygenase (thromboxane A2) for the platelet's lifespan; clopidogrel blocks the P2Y12 ADP receptor. Defects: Bernard–Soulier syndrome (GPIb deficiency), Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb/IIIa deficiency) and von Willebrand disease (the commonest inherited bleeding disorder).

material.heading: Coagulation and fibrinolysis
material.body: Secondary haemostasis forms a stable fibrin clot. The classical cascade: extrinsic pathway (tissue factor + factor VIIa — measured by PT), intrinsic pathway (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII — measured by APTT) and common pathway (X, V, II (prothrombin), I (fibrinogen)); thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin and activates factor XIII, which cross-links fibrin. The cell-based model describes initiation (tissue factor on cells), amplification (thrombin activates platelets and cofactors V and VIII) and propagation (large thrombin burst on platelet surfaces). Vitamin K-dependent factors: II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S (warfarin antagonises vitamin K). Natural anticoagulants: antithrombin (inhibits thrombin and Xa — potentiated by heparin), protein C and protein S (inactivate Va and VIIIa), and tissue factor pathway inhibitor. Fibrinolysis: plasminogen is converted to plasmin by tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), degrading fibrin into fibrin degradation products including D-dimer; tranexamic acid inhibits fibrinolysis.
keyPoints: Vitamin K factors II, VII, IX, X, C, S

topics.title: Laboratory Investigation of Bleeding Disorders
topics.summary: Sample collection, screening tests, mixing studies, factor assays and interpretation.

material.heading: Pre-analytical and screening tests
material.body: Coagulation samples are collected in 3.2% sodium citrate tubes filled to the correct level (9:1 blood-to-anticoagulant ratio — underfilling prolongs results; high haematocrit > 55% needs citrate adjustment), with clean venepuncture, avoiding heparin contamination from lines, and tested within about 4 hours. Screening tests: platelet count and blood film (clumping causes pseudothrombocytopenia — EDTA-dependent; check film), PT/INR, APTT, thrombin time (fibrinogen function; prolonged by heparin), fibrinogen (Clauss method), and D-dimer. Interpretation: prolonged PT only — factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease; prolonged APTT only — haemophilia A/B, factor XI or XII deficiency (XII — no bleeding), vWD, heparin, lupus anticoagulant (paradoxically thrombotic); both prolonged — common pathway deficiency, DIC, liver disease, warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, massive transfusion. Platelet function testing (aggregometry, PFA-100) investigates platelet disorders; the bleeding time is obsolete.
keyPoints: APTT only: VIII, IX, XI, XII, heparin, LA

material.heading: Further tests
material.body: Mixing studies distinguish factor deficiency from inhibitors: patient plasma mixed 1:1 with normal pooled plasma — correction indicates deficiency; failure to correct indicates an inhibitor (lupus anticoagulant, acquired factor VIII inhibitor — acquired haemophilia, or heparin). Specific factor assays (one-stage clotting assays for VIII, IX, etc.) quantify deficiency: haemophilia severity — severe < 1%, moderate 1–5%, mild > 5–40% factor activity. Von Willebrand disease tests: vWF antigen, vWF activity (ristocetin cofactor/GPIb binding), factor VIII and multimer analysis (types 1 — partial quantitative deficiency; 2 — qualitative; 3 — severe). Inhibitor quantification uses the Bethesda assay. Lupus anticoagulant is confirmed with dilute Russell's viper venom time (DRVVT) and phospholipid-dependent tests. Quality control and participation in EQA are essential in haemostasis laboratories.

topics.title: Thrombosis and Anticoagulant Monitoring
topics.summary: Thrombophilia, DIC, antiphospholipid syndrome, and monitoring heparin, warfarin and DOACs.

material.heading: Thrombotic disorders
material.body: Virchow's triad: stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. Inherited thrombophilias: factor V Leiden (resistance to activated protein C — rare in Africans), prothrombin G20210A, and deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C and protein S. Acquired: antiphospholipid syndrome (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies — venous/arterial thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss), malignancy, pregnancy and the puerperium, oral contraceptives, surgery, immobility, sickle cell disease, nephrotic syndrome and HIV. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (sepsis, obstetric complications — abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, retained dead fetus; trauma, snakebite envenoming — carpet viper; APL): consumption of platelets and factors — low platelets, prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer, fragmented red cells on film; treat the cause and replace products (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate). Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT — fall in platelets 5–10 days after heparin, with thrombosis; stop heparin, use non-heparin anticoagulant; 4T score and anti-PF4 antibodies).
keyPoints: Factor V Leiden rare in Africans
DIC: low platelets and fibrinogen, high D-dimer

material.heading: Anticoagulant monitoring
material.body: Unfractionated heparin: monitored by APTT (ratio about 1.5–2.5) or anti-Xa assay; reversed by protamine. Low-molecular-weight heparins (enoxaparin): predictable, usually no monitoring; anti-Xa in renal impairment, pregnancy, extremes of weight. Warfarin: monitored by INR (PT ratio corrected with ISI — target usually 2.0–3.0; 2.5–3.5 for mechanical mitral valves); interactions (antibiotics, antifungals, herbal products) and diet affect INR; reversal — omit doses, vitamin K, prothrombin complex concentrate or FFP for major bleeding. Direct oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban, apixaban — anti-Xa; dabigatran — direct thrombin inhibitor): no routine monitoring; drug-specific anti-Xa levels or dilute thrombin time when needed; reversal agents andexanet alfa and idarucizumab (limited availability in Nigeria). Point-of-care INR devices support anticoagulation clinics.

topics.title: Laboratory Diagnosis of Leukaemias
topics.summary: Blood film, bone marrow, cytochemistry, immunophenotyping and cytogenetics in leukaemia diagnosis.

material.heading: Acute leukaemia
material.body: Acute leukaemias present with bone marrow failure (anaemia, infections, bleeding) and blasts in blood and marrow (≥ 20% blasts in marrow or blood — WHO). Differentiating AML from ALL: morphology (myeloblasts — larger, more cytoplasm, granules, Auer rods (pathognomonic of myeloid lineage); lymphoblasts — small, scanty cytoplasm, no granules), cytochemistry (myeloperoxidase and Sudan black B positive in AML; PAS block positivity in ALL; non-specific esterase in monocytic AML), and immunophenotyping by flow cytometry (myeloid — CD13, CD33, CD117, MPO; B-ALL — CD19, CD10, CD79a, TdT; T-ALL — CD3, CD7, TdT). Cytogenetics and molecular tests guide prognosis and therapy: t(15;17) PML-RARA (acute promyelocytic leukaemia — DIC; treat with ATRA ± arsenic trioxide), t(8;21) and inv(16) (favourable AML), t(9;22) BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia-positive ALL — poorer prognosis, tyrosine kinase inhibitors), t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1 (favourable childhood ALL). Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy assess cellularity and infiltration.

material.heading: Chronic leukaemias and MPNs
material.body: Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML): very high white cell count with the full spectrum of myeloid maturation (myelocytes, metamyelocytes), basophilia, often thrombocytosis, massive splenomegaly; Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) and BCR-ABL1 fusion confirmed by karyotype, FISH or RT-PCR; quantitative BCR-ABL1 PCR monitors response to imatinib (major molecular response). Phases: chronic, accelerated and blast crisis. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL): elderly, lymphocytosis of small mature lymphocytes with smudge (smear) cells; immunophenotype CD5+, CD19+, CD23+, weak surface immunoglobulin (Matutes score); staging by Rai or Binet. Myeloproliferative neoplasms: polycythaemia vera (raised haematocrit; JAK2 V617F in > 95%), essential thrombocythaemia (JAK2, CALR, MPL), and primary myelofibrosis (teardrop cells, leucoerythroblastic film, dry tap). Leucoerythroblastic blood films (nucleated red cells and immature myeloid cells) suggest marrow infiltration (metastases, myelofibrosis, TB) or severe stress.

topics.title: Lymphomas, Myeloma and Bone Marrow Examination
topics.summary: Lymphoma diagnosis, plasma cell disorders, and bone marrow sampling and reporting.

material.heading: Lymphomas and myeloma
material.body: Lymphomas are diagnosed on lymph node excision biopsy (preferred to FNAC for architecture), with histology and immunohistochemistry. Hodgkin lymphoma: Reed–Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+, CD45−) in an inflammatory background; staging Ann Arbor I–IV with B symptoms. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (commonest), follicular lymphoma (t(14;18) BCL2), Burkitt lymphoma (t(8;14) MYC; 'starry sky' pattern; Ki-67 ~100%; endemic in African children — EBV and malaria), and HIV-associated lymphomas. Multiple myeloma: clonal plasma cells ≥ 10% in marrow plus CRAB features (hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone lesions) or biomarkers; investigations — serum protein electrophoresis (M-band/paraprotein) with immunofixation, serum free light chains, urine Bence Jones protein, rouleaux on blood film, raised ESR, skeletal survey or low-dose CT; MGUS is the precursor (< 10% plasma cells, no end-organ damage). Myeloma is relatively more common in people of African descent.

material.heading: Bone marrow examination
material.body: Bone marrow aspiration and trephine biopsy are usually taken from the posterior iliac crest (sternal aspiration only in adults, never trephine). Aspirate smears (Romanowsky stains) assess cellular morphology and the myeloid:erythroid (M:E) ratio (normal about 2–4:1), blast percentage, dysplasia, infiltration and iron stores (Perls' stain — ring sideroblasts in sideroblastic anaemia and MDS); aspirate is also sent for flow cytometry, cytogenetics, molecular tests and microbiology (TB, leishmaniasis — Leishman–Donovan bodies, histoplasmosis). The trephine (processed histologically) assesses cellularity (roughly 100 minus age %), architecture, fibrosis (reticulin stain), and focal infiltrates (lymphoma, metastatic carcinoma, granulomas). Indications: unexplained cytopenias, suspected leukaemia or lymphoma staging, myeloma, pyrexia of unknown origin, and storage diseases. Complications are rare (bleeding, infection, pain).
